newsitem.title: GUATEMALA: Rebellion means Guatemala army not ready for peace.
newsitem.headline: Rebellion means Guatemala army not ready for peace.

text.p: A five-day rebellion by military police, which ended on Sunday, showed the army was not completely prepared for peace, analysts said on Monday.
"This dangerous and violent event reflects that the old militarism has not died yet and the new army has not been born yet," leftist congressman Amilcar Mendez told Reuters.

Hundreds of Guatemalan military police seized their own barracks on Wednesday night and refused to turn in their weapons for five days, insisting the government promise them severance pay when they lose their jobs later this year.
The crisis reached its height on Saturday when the military police briefly took a general hostage during a gunfight with troops in armoured vehicles surrounding the barracks.
The soldiers and armoured vehicles had withdrawn by Monday and the military police, apparently cowed by the army's display of heavy artillery, returned to their regular duties.

Mendez said the government should have anticipated the uprising and taken steps to prepare military police for changes that would come as the Guatemalan army adjusted to the end of 36 years of civil war.

The entire 4,000-member military police force will be disbanded this year as part of army cuts the government promised when it signed peace accords on Dec. 29 with leftist rebels the Guatemalan National Revolutionary Unit (URNG).
The revolt marked the first sign of military discontent over terms of the peace accord, which also eliminates the army's traditional role in internal security.
Backed by the rightwing ruling class, the army has long been a unified monolith of power. Military dictators or puppet presidents ensured the institution's strength for decades.
During the civil war, the armed forces killed and tortured tens of thousands of civilians in counterinsurgency campaigns.
Government officials, who downplayed the rebellion from the beginning, continued to minimise its importance.
"This was an unanticipated setback but it will not affect the process of fulfilling the peace accords," Defence Minister Gen. Julio Balconi told Reuters.
Balconi said the army would analyse whether the military police would be subject to discipline or criminal charges.
Balconi said there was no risk of more rebellions since the military police was the only unit of the armed forces that would be demobilized entirely under peace accords.
He said other army reductions would come as soldiers completed their service.
But Guatemalan Nobel Peace Prize laureate Rigoberta Menchu, a strong critic of the army, warned that the spirit of the uprising could catch on among other army units.
The rebellion included scenes of rare insubordination. At one point military police armed with assault rifles heckled and shoved three generals who had arrived to negotiate.

Even though the revolt ended on Sunday, the military police apparently are still demanding severance pay. A government negotiating team will examine other options with the military police, including a job training proposal.
